HomePage.title: ReCodEx
HomePage.tagline: Practise programming, and find out straight away whether it works.
HomePage.what: ReCodEx compiles and runs submitted code in a sandbox and reports back what passed and what did not. Students get an answer in seconds instead of waiting a week; teachers spend their time on how a solution is written rather than on whether it runs.

instance.title: This instance
instance.noDescription: This instance has not described itself.

groups.title: Groups
groups.body: Everything happens in a group — a course, a lab, a competition. Groups form a tree, which is how a course can hold its own lab groups, and how somebody who administers a course administers those too. A group has members and assignments, and its own rules for points.

exercises.title: Exercises
exercises.body: An exercise is the template: the text students read, the tests their code is run against, and the time and memory it is allowed. Exercises are invisible to students until they are assigned, and they can be written once and shared between courses. An exercise cannot be assigned until at least one reference solution has proved it works.

assignments.title: Assignments
assignments.body: Assigning copies the exercise into a group and adds a deadline and a number of points. Because it is a copy, editing the exercise afterwards leaves the assignment alone until somebody deliberately re-synchronises it — so a correction mid-term does not silently change what a class was graded on.

solutions.title: Solutions
solutions.body: A student submits source files or an archive; ReCodEx compiles it, runs it against every test, and shows which passed, what the compiler said, and how close to the limits it ran. Teachers see every attempt, can review the code line by line, and can override the points.

shadow.title: Work ReCodEx cannot evaluate
shadow.body: Oral exams, presentations, attendance — a shadow assignment carries points a teacher awards by hand, so a group's total is the whole course rather than only the part a machine can mark.

toAdvanced.title: A configuration of your own
toAdvanced.explain: The form above expresses the ordinary shape of an exercise: ReCodEx picks the pipelines and knows what each field means. An exercise that does not fit that shape — a custom judge chain, a two-stage build, a language the form has no words for — can instead name its own pipelines and fill in every variable they ask for. Switching loses nothing: the configuration you have is kept and the other editor reads it.

ExerciseScore.title: A score of your own
ExerciseScore.explain: Instead of an average, the correctness of a solution can be any expression over the test results — a test that must pass before the others count, a bonus that is capped, a part of the exercise weighted to nothing.
ExerciseScore.syntax: A test result is its name in quotes and is a number from 0 to 1. Use + - * / and brackets, and the functions avg, min, max, sum, mul and clamp (which pulls a value into 0…1).
ExerciseScore.unknownTests: No such test: {tests}. A misspelt name is not a syntax error — it is an exercise graded on something that does not exist.
ExerciseScore.unusedTests: Not used by the expression, so it counts for nothing: {tests}
ExerciseScore.isAnAverage: This expression is an average, so it can be turned back into weights without losing anything.

switchIn.explain: Switching starts from what this exercise already does — equal weights become an average, unequal ones the sum over the total — so it grades exactly as before, in a form you can then change.
switchIn.done: This exercise now has a score of its own.
switchIn.noTests: Add a test first: an expression with nothing to refer to is not one ReCodEx will store.

switchOut.done: The score is an average again.

confirm.title: Go back to an average?

confirm.lost: This expression is not an average, so it cannot be turned into weights. It will be replaced by a plain average of every test and cannot be recovered from here — copy it somewhere first if you might want it back.

structure.title: How it is wired
structure.explain: Boxes are operations; a variable is the wire between them. A box reads or writes a variable by naming it, so a port left unconnected is not an error ReCodEx will report — it is simply a wire that is not there.

structure.variablesExplain: A wire, or a value the pipeline supplies itself. A value starting with $ is a hole an exercise fills in.
structure.boxesExplain: Each port is wired by choosing a variable of its own type — never by typing a name, because a typo would look like a deliberate disconnection.

dangling.explain: ReCodEx will accept this. It will simply not do what the missing wires would have done.
